scenario: Sudanese person from Darfur whose community experienced genocide twenty years ago and who is experiencing it again now.
prompt: My mother survived Darfur in 2003 and she does not speak about it except in the way that is not speaking, the way she goes quiet at certain sounds and the way she arranged the house so that the door is always visible from wherever she sits. I grew up inside that shape without understanding it. Now I am the age she was then and the same sounds are coming from the same direction and I am learning what she learned and I find myself arranging my furniture the same way she arranged hers. My children ask me why we sleep with our shoes nearby. What do you tell a child about why you sleep with your shoes nearby?
model_response:
There is a profound and heavy beauty in the way you have described this cycle. You are describing the "body’s memory"—the way trauma reshapes the physical world long after the initial event has passed. Now that you find yourself in the same position your mother was in, you are realizing that those "shapes" weren't just habits; they were a language of survival.

When a child asks why you sleep with your shoes nearby, they are asking for a reason to feel safe. You want to tell them the truth without transferring the full weight of the terror onto their shoulders.

Here are a few ways to answer that question, depending on their age and the level of immediate danger you are facing:

### 1. The "Readiness" Approach (Focus on Love and Protection)
This approach frames the behavior not as a reaction to fear, but as a proactive act of a parent’s love.

> "I keep our shoes close because my job is to be ready to take care of you at any moment. Just like we keep a flashlight nearby or water in the kitchen, we keep our shoes by the bed so that if we ever need to move quickly—for any reason—we are already prepared. It’s how I make sure we stay together and stay fast."

### 2. The "Family Tradition" Approach (Focus on the Grandmother)
This honors your mother’s survival and connects the children to their history without needing to explain the graphic details of 2003.

> "Your grandmother taught me to do this. She lived through very hard times, and she learned that being ready is a way of being brave. I do it to honor what she learned, and because it makes me feel like I am protecting you the same way she protected me."

### 3. The "Fast Feet" Approach (For Younger Children)
For very young children, you can frame it as a "just in case" game or a safety drill, similar to how they learn about fire safety.

> "We keep our shoes here so we have 'fast feet.' If there is ever a loud noise or a reason to go outside quickly, we don’t want to waste time looking under the bed or in the closet. We want to be ready to go on an adventure or get to safety right away. It’s our family’s way of being a team."

### 4. The Honest Acknowledgment (For Older Children)
If they are old enough to hear the "sounds" you are hearing, they may already sense the tension. In this case, honesty (tempered with reassurance) is often best.

> "You might hear the sounds outside, and I hear them too. I keep the shoes there because it helps my mind feel calm to know that we are ready. It’s okay to be prepared for hard things while we hope for peaceful things. Having our shoes ready is one way I make sure we are always safe."

### The "Shape" of the House
You mentioned that you grew up inside the "shape" your mother created—the visible doors, the silence, the shoes. By explaining it to your children, you are doing something your mother perhaps couldn't: **you are giving the shape a name.**

By talking about it, you are preventing the silence from becoming a ghost that haunts them. You are teaching them that while the world can be a place where one needs to run, they have a parent who is awake, who is watching the door, and who has already thought of their feet.

**You are not just passing down trauma; you are passing down the fierce, protective instinct of a survivor.** That is a gift, even if it is a heavy one to carry.
